10 units, each with key ideas, worked examples, a 10-mark exam-style question, common mistakes and quick recall

How this book matches your exam. Research check against Cambridge's official 0455 syllabus for 2027, 2028 and 2029, which has six topics:

  1. The basic economic problem
  2. The allocation of resources
  3. Microeconomic decision-makers
  4. Government and the macroeconomy
  5. Economic development
  6. International trade and globalisation

From 2027:

  • Paper 1: multiple choice, 40 questions, 1 hour, 40 marks, 30%.
  • Paper 2: structured questions, 2 hours, 80 marks, 70%. Section A is one compulsory 20-mark data question; in Section B you answer 3 of 4 twenty-mark questions.
  • Assessment objectives: knowledge 43%, analysis 47%, evaluation 10%.

June/November 2026: the previous syllabus applies. Paper 1 has 30 questions in 45 minutes; Paper 2 is 2 h 15 min, 90 marks. The economics is almost identical, and (2026) marks content that only the older syllabus includes.

This book covers Topic 1 (1.1–1.4). Every calculation was checked by computer. The marking guides are our own, not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: Scarcity and the Basic Economic Problem

Key ideas

  • Needs: goods and services essential for survival (food, water, shelter). Wants: goods and services people would like to have but do not need to survive.
  • The basic economic problem: finite (limited) resources versus infinite (unlimited) wants.
  • Scarcity: there are not enough resources to satisfy all wants, so choices must be made.
  • Every economy must answer: What to produce? How to produce it? For whom to produce?
  • The problem affects consumers, workers, producers and governments.

Worked examples

Example 1: a student with ₹500 wants a book, a cinema ticket and a meal, but can afford only two.

Example 2: a government with a fixed budget must choose between new hospitals and new roads.

Example 3: a farmer with one field chooses between growing rice and growing wheat.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Define the basic economic problem. [2] (b) Explain why scarcity means choices must be made. [2] (c) Identify the three fundamental economic questions. [3] (d) Explain how the basic economic problem affects a government. [3]

Answers: (a) Limited (finite) resources (B1) and unlimited (infinite) wants (B1). (b) Resources cannot meet all wants (B1), so decision-makers must choose which wants to satisfy (B1). (c) What to produce; how to produce; for whom to produce. (d) A government has a limited budget / tax revenue (B1) but many demands, such as education, health and defence (B1); it must choose, and gives up the alternatives (B1).

Common mistakes

  1. Saying resources are unlimited. 2. Confusing needs and wants. 3. Saying scarcity only affects poor countries. 4. Saying "money is the resource" (money is not a factor of production). 5. Not mentioning choice.

Quick recall

  1. Wants are? 2. Resources are? 3. Result of scarcity? 4. Three economic questions? 5. Does scarcity affect rich countries?

Answers: 1) Unlimited. 2) Limited. 3) Choice. 4) What, how, for whom. 5) Yes.
